Obsidian Plugin Review Checker

Scans your plugin's manifest.json, versions.json, and JavaScript/TypeScript source for the patterns behind common Obsidian community-plugin review delays: missing required manifest fields, leftover sample-plugin template placeholder values, a manifest version with no matching versions.json entry, and innerHTML/outerHTML/insertAdjacentHTML usage. Everything runs in this tab; nothing is uploaded. A command-line version for CI is in the same repository (node check.mjs .).


Pick your plugin's project folder (includes manifest.json, versions.json, and your .js/.ts source). Not at your project right now? instead.

No folder selected yet.

Common questions

Why does a missing versions.json entry matter for an Obsidian plugin release?

Obsidian's release mechanism reads versions.json to decide which installed app versions can see a given plugin release. manifest.json only carries the current version; versions.json has to carry its own matching entry, in a separate file, with nothing forcing the two to move together. This tool reads both and tells you if the current version is missing.

What are the sample-plugin placeholder values this tool flags?

The official obsidian-sample-plugin GitHub template ships manifest.json with id "sample-plugin", name "Sample Plugin", and author "Your Name". A submission that still carries any of these has not customized the template it was generated from -- a leftover reviewers name explicitly.

Why does innerHTML/outerHTML/insertAdjacentHTML matter in an Obsidian plugin?

Obsidian's own developer guidelines name these APIs as a cross-site-scripting risk and recommend the DOM API or Obsidian's own createEl/createSpan/createDiv helpers instead. This tool scans for the assignment or call regardless of whether the specific value used happens to be attacker-controlled today -- the fix is standard, and reviewers ask for it as a matter of course.

Is my plugin's source code uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser tool reads the files or folder you select using the File API and never sends them anywhere -- everything happens in memory in your tab. The CLI never makes a network call either.

Does a clean report mean my plugin will be approved for the community plugin list?

No. This is evidence from pattern-matching your manifest.json, versions.json, and source against known field names and API calls -- it is not the review process, and it is a line-level heuristic, not data-flow or runtime analysis. It can miss an innerHTML assignment built from a value that is actually safe, a registerDomEvent call the reviewer would still ask about for an unrelated reason, or a guideline this tool does not check at all. Always re-check against Obsidian's current developer guidelines before submitting.

More on the most common of these: Fixing a missing versions.json entry.

Already using ESLint? See how this checker compares to eslint-plugin-obsidianmd, the official Obsidian ESLint plugin.

Evidence, not a determination. This tool reports what pattern-matching found in the folder you selected -- known manifest/versions field names, and known risky API calls. It is a line-level heuristic, not data-flow or runtime analysis: it cannot confirm an innerHTML value is actually attacker-controlled, that a direct event listener really leaks across reloads, or that a field spelled non-standardly is really absent rather than just unrecognized. A clean report is not a guarantee your plugin will be approved for the community plugin list -- verify against Obsidian's current plugin guidelines before you submit.

versions-json-missing-entry.html.text:
Fixing a missing versions.json entry

A community plugin release with no matching entry in versions.json is one of the easiest release-blocking mistakes to introduce, because manifest.json and versions.json live in two separate files, in two different formats, with nothing forcing them to move together.

Why it happens

Obsidian's release mechanism reads versions.json to decide which installed app versions can see a given plugin release. manifest.json carries only the current release's version and its minAppVersion -- it says nothing about history. Bump the version in manifest.json, tag the release, and forget to add the matching line to versions.json, and the release exists but the version-resolution step it depends on does not know about it.

What "correct" looks like

FileExampleWhat it controls
manifest.json"version": "1.4.0"The current release's version string
versions.json{ "1.4.0": "0.15.0" }Which Obsidian app versions the release is compatible with

Every version you have ever released should keep its own entry in versions.json -- it only grows, it never has old versions removed, since a user on an older Obsidian build may still need to know which of your past releases it can run.

Find it automatically

The checker on this site reads both files and tells you immediately if the current version has no matching entry, along with the other checks it runs (required manifest fields, leftover sample-plugin placeholder values, and the innerHTML/outerHTML/ insertAdjacentHTML pattern Obsidian's own developer guidelines flag). It runs as a browser tool (nothing uploaded) or a Node CLI you can add to your own pre-release check.

This is evidence of what the two files currently say, not a determination that a community-plugin submission will be approved in every respect -- see the checker and its disclaimer for what else it can and can't see, and verify against Obsidian's current plugin guidelines before you submit or tag a release.

vs-eslint-plugin-obsidianmd.html.text:
← Back to the Obsidian Plugin Review Checker

Obsidian Plugin Review Checker vs. eslint-plugin-obsidianmd

eslint-plugin-obsidianmd is the official Obsidian team's ESLint plugin -- maintained under the obsidianmd GitHub organization, with around 40 rules that check a plugin's TypeScript/JavaScript source against the full range of Obsidian's developer guidelines. It is the deeper, broader tool, and it is meant to live inside a plugin's own project as a permanent lint step, not to be run once from a browser tab. This checker is a narrower, zero-install pre-flight pass for the specific patterns that most commonly delay a first community-plugin review.

What actually differs

Setup eslint-plugin-obsidianmd is installed with npm install eslint-plugin-obsidianmd --save-dev into an existing project, plus ESLint itself and an eslint.config.mjs; its type-checked rules also need a TypeScript-aware parser configuration. This checker needs none of that: open index.html and pick your plugin's folder, or run node check.mjs . from the plugin's directory with no config file at all.
versions.json cross-check eslint-plugin-obsidianmd's validate-manifest rule checks manifest.json's own structure, but none of its ~40 rules cross-check the current manifest version against versions.json's own entries -- versions.json is a separate file that ESLint, which lints source and config files, has no reason to open. This checker reads both files and reports it directly.
Breadth eslint-plugin-obsidianmd's ~40 rules cover command naming, settings-tab patterns, sentence case in UI strings, API-version compatibility, and a long list of DOM and platform API preferences -- far more than this checker looks at. This checker covers five things: required manifest fields, sample-plugin template leftovers, the versions.json entry, and innerHTML/outerHTML/insertAdjacentHTML usage.
When you'd reach for each eslint-plugin-obsidianmd running on every commit in CI, for a project already set up with ESLint and TypeScript. This checker for a quick pass before a first submission, or when you just want an answer without touching the project's own lint configuration.

What does not differ

Both tools exist because Obsidian's own published developer guidelines name these as review blockers, and both read from the same public documentation. Neither is the review process, and a clean report from either is not a guarantee of approval -- see this checker's own disclaimer on index.html, and verify against Obsidian's current plugin guidelines before you submit either way.

Common questions

Does eslint-plugin-obsidianmd already check my versions.json against manifest.json?

No. Its validate-manifest rule checks the structure of manifest.json on its own, and its sample-names and no-sample-code rules catch leftover sample-plugin template code, but none of its rules cross-check manifest.json's current version against versions.json's own entries. That specific cross-file check is what this tool's versions.json entry check does.

Do I need to set up ESLint to use this checker?

No. eslint-plugin-obsidianmd is installed with npm into an existing project and needs an eslint.config.mjs, plus a TypeScript-aware parser configuration for its type-checked rules. This checker needs none of that: open index.html and pick your plugin's folder, or run node check.mjs . from the plugin's own directory with no config file at all.

Should I use this tool or eslint-plugin-obsidianmd?

Both, for different jobs. eslint-plugin-obsidianmd is the deeper tool: around 40 rules covering the full range of Obsidian's developer guidelines -- command naming, settings-tab patterns, sentence case in UI strings, API version compatibility, and more -- wired into your project's own lint step so it runs on every change. This tool is a narrower, five-check pre-flight pass with zero setup: required manifest fields, sample-plugin template leftovers, the versions.json entry, and innerHTML/outerHTML/insertAdjacentHTML usage. Running this tool once before a first submission does not require touching your project's ESLint configuration at all.

Is this page affiliated with Obsidian or the eslint-plugin-obsidianmd maintainers?

No. This page is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Obsidian or Dynalist Inc. eslint-plugin-obsidianmd is maintained under the obsidianmd GitHub organization; it is named here only to describe what it is and is not, based on its own public repository and README.

vs-guessing-or-waiting-for-review.html.text:
← Obsidian Plugin Review Checker

This checker vs. guessing from Obsidian's guidelines or waiting for a reviewer to comment

Obsidian's developer guidelines name the required manifest.json fields, explain that versions.json needs its own matching entry for the current version, and call out innerHTML/outerHTML/insertAdjacentHTML as a cross-site-scripting risk to avoid. What they do not do is read your specific manifest.json, your specific versions.json, or your specific source files and tell you which one you actually got wrong, in which file, on which line. That cross-check has always meant either a guess informed by the docs, or a definite answer from a reviewer's comment on your pull request days later.

What each approach actually gives you

Obsidian's documentation is complete and authoritative about what the requirements are. It is not a scanner: it cannot look at your project and tell you that your manifest.json still carries the sample plugin's "id": "sample-plugin", because it has never seen your files.

A reviewer's comment will eventually tell you, with certainty -- after you open a pull request in obsidianmd/obsidian-releases, wait for it to be read, and get a comment naming the exact field or line. For a versions.json entry that quietly fell out of sync with manifest.json, that comment may be the first time anyone notices.

This checker runs the same field, placeholder, and API checks a reviewer would, against your manifest, your versions.json, and your source, before you submit -- in the browser (nothing uploaded) or as a Node CLI you can gate CI on.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Which field, placeholder, or API call is the problem, and where?This checker's scan -- file and line, free, nothing uploaded.
What are the required manifest fields and their names?This checker lists them; both it and Obsidian's docs agree, since this tool's field list is checked against Obsidian's published guidelines.
Will the community plugin list actually approve my submission?Neither. Only Obsidian's own review determines that -- this is evidence about your files as they stand today.
Is my plugin's source code uploaded anywhere?No. The browser tool reads files with the File API; the CLI never makes a network call.

Common questions

Doesn't Obsidian's own developer documentation already cover this?

It lists the required manifest.json fields, explains that versions.json needs its own matching entry for the current version, and names innerHTML/outerHTML/insertAdjacentHTML as a cross-site-scripting risk to avoid. What it doesn't do is read your specific manifest.json, your specific versions.json, or your specific source files and tell you which one you actually got wrong, in which file, on which line. That cross-check is what used to mean either guessing from the docs or finding out from a reviewer's comment.

What does waiting for a reviewer's comment actually cost?

A round trip on your pull request in obsidian-releases, at minimum -- open a submission, wait for a maintainer or bot to read it, get a comment naming the exact field or line, push a fix, and wait again. For a plugin id or author field still carrying the obsidian-sample-plugin template's default value, or a versions.json entry that quietly fell out of sync with manifest.json, that comment may be the first time anyone notices. Scanning before you open the pull request catches the same defect without spending a review round trip to find it.

Can I just search my code and manifest by hand for these patterns?

You can, and for a small plugin it may be faster than downloading a tool. The risk is coverage: six required manifest fields, three template placeholder values, a versions.json cross-reference, and three DOM APIs to grep for across every .js/.ts/.jsx/.tsx file in the project -- easy to miss one on a plugin with more than a couple of source files. This tool runs the same checks against every file you point it at, in the browser or as a CI-gating CLI, so a placeholder or an unsafe assignment buried in a file you didn't think to check is not the one a reviewer finds first.

Does a clean report from this tool guarantee my plugin gets approved?

No, and it is not built to. This is pattern-matching against known manifest/versions.json field names and known risky API calls in the files you point it at -- a line-level heuristic, not data-flow or runtime analysis. It can miss an innerHTML assignment built from a genuinely safe value, or a guideline this tool does not check at all. A clean report means your current files agree with the specific patterns this tool checks; it is not a guarantee of approval, so verify against Obsidian's current plugin guidelines before you submit.
